content:
Apple is citing a recently paused securities fraud lawsuit to support its request to pause further lower court proceedings in its legal battle with Epic Games, while the Supreme Court considers some of the disputes. Details below.

Apple points to the relevant ruling; Judge Rogers is considering the pause request

Earlier this year, a proposed class action on behalf of the Coral Springs Police Officers Pension Plan was filed against Apple, alleging securities fraud.

The lawsuit accused Apple of misleading investors, including about whether the company was truly complying with the injunction in the Epic Games case, and whether it would deliver its announced AI-powered Siri features on schedule.

Meanwhile, Apple continues to challenge the contempt of court ruling in the Epic case. The Supreme Court is now considering whether Apple can be held in civil contempt for continuing to collect commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, after a 2021 injunction required it to allow external payment options — an injunction that did not explicitly prohibit such fees.

Last week, Apple asked the lower court to pause proceedings to clarify what commissions (if any) the company may collect on purchases made outside the App Store, pending the Supreme Court's review of the contempt ruling.

Apple argued that the Supreme Court's ruling could affect the lower court proceedings, but Epic Games objected.

It turns out Apple had made a similar pause request in the Coral Springs securities fraud case, since that case also involves the Epic Games case.

Earlier today, Judge Noël Wise granted Apple's request, meaning the Coral Springs case will remain paused until the Supreme Court rules on the civil contempt decision.

Apple then promptly submitted Judge Wise's ruling in the Epic case to the court, arguing that the ruling supports its request to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to pause proceedings.

Apple's filing to Judge Rogers:

Judge Rogers is now considering Apple's arguments in favor of a pause, as well as Epic's arguments against it. Apple is hoping Judge Wise's ruling will persuade Judge Rogers to reach the same decision.

Worth noting, in its filing responding to Epic's opposition to pausing the case, Apple also asked Judge Gonzalez Rogers to hold off on proceedings even if the pause request is denied, so the company could seek to continue freezing the case at the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court, while awaiting the Supreme Court's separate review of the contempt ruling.
